text: Kara Elizabeth Walker, born on November 26, 1969, in Stockton, California, is an American contemporary artist known for her work in painting, silhouettist, printmaking, installation art, filmmaking, and teaching. She explores themes of race, gender, sexuality, violence, and identity, with her most recognized works being large-scale, room-size tableaux of black cut-paper silhouettes that depict the history of American slavery and racism through violent and unsettling imagery. Walker earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts (BFA) from the Atlanta College of Art in 1991 and a Master of Fine Arts (MFA) in painting from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1994. She was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship in 1997 at the age of 28, becoming one of the youngest recipients of the award, second only to David Stuart. Since 2015, she has held the Tepper Chair in Visual Arts at the Mason Gross School of the Arts, Rutgers University. Walker’s early life in an integrated California suburb was described as calm, with no early indicators of her future artistic path. At age 13, her father, Larry Walker, a painter and professor, accepted a position at Georgia State University, leading the family to Stone Mountain, Georgia, where the presence of Ku Klux Klan rallies and racial hostility deeply impacted her. Walker recalls being called a "nigger," told she looked like a monkey, and accused of being a "Yankee" at her new high school. Her work draws on historical textbooks to show how enslaved African Americans were depicted in the Antebellum South, using the genteel tradition of silhouettes to create nightmarish scenes that reveal the brutality of American racism. Influenced by artists such as Andy Warhol, Adrian Piper, and Robert Colescott, Walker’s art often incorporates sharp, ominous elements like Spanish moss and a giant moon obscured by clouds, creating a circular, claustrophobic space reminiscent of 19th-century cycloramas. Notable works include her 1994 mural *Gone, An Historical Romance of a Civil War as It Occurred Between the Dusky Thighs of One Young Negress and Her Heart*, which references *Gone with the Wind* and Walt Disney’s fairy-tale imagery, and her 2014 public installation *A Subtlety, or the Marvelous Sugar Baby, an Homage to the unpaid and overworked Artisans who have refined our Sweet tastes from the cane fields to the Kitchens of the New World on the Occasion of the demolition of the Domino Sugar Refining Plant*, a 75-foot-long, 35-foot-high female sphinx made of 80 tons of white sugar, preceded by fifteen life-size figures—five in solid sugar and ten in molasses-coated resin—standing 60 inches tall and weighing 300–500 pounds each. The installation, commissioned by Creative Time and displayed at the Domino Sugar Refinery in Brooklyn, attracted over 130,000 visitors and was demolished after its eight-weekend run in July 2014. Walker has also created *Insurrection! (Our Tools Were Rudimentary, Yet We Pressed On)* (2000), which uses colored light projections evocative of 1930s animated films, and *8 Possible Beginnings* (2005), which incorporates moving images, sound, and her own and her daughter’s voices to explore the legacy of slavery. In 2016, she produced *Slaughter of the Innocents (They Might be Guilty of Something)*, depicting an African American woman slicing a baby, inspired by Margaret Garner’s act of killing her daughter to prevent re-enslavement. In 2019, she created *Fons Americanus* for Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, a 13-foot fountain referencing African, American, and European histories, including specific artworks like *The Slave Ship* by J.M.W. Turner and *The Gulf Stream* by Winslow Homer, and drawing on the tradition of public monuments to emphasize dread as a tool for remembering historical trauma. In 2023, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art commissioned her first site-specific installation for its Roberts Family Gallery. In 2025, Walker was one of the artists commissioned to create a work for the MONUMENTS exhibition at The Geffen Contemporary at MOCA and The Brick, co-curating the exhibit with Hamza Walker and Bennett Simpson, which marked a historic moment in the context of monument removals. Walker describes her artistic process as “two parts research and one part paranoid hysteria,” emphasizing the entanglement of history and fantasy. She has stated that she wants viewers to engage actively, not passively, and that her work aims to provoke reactions such as nervous laughter, immersion in history, or discomfort, while also being “overwhelmingly beautiful and intellectually compelling.” Her work has been widely recognized as among the most prominent and acclaimed Black American artists working today. A major retrospective of her drawings and archival materials was held at Kustmuseum Basel in 2021. In 2007, her exhibition *Kara Walker: My Complement, My Oppressor, My Enemy, My Love* was her first full-scale U.S. museum survey. Walker has also created site-specific installations such as *An Abbreviated Emancipation* (2002) at the University of Michigan Museum of Art and *Event Horizon* (2005) at The New School. In 1998/1999, she participated in a season in Vienna.

Dread, for Kara Walker, functions as an engine that drives memory and a rightful fear of the ruins we should not return to or re-create—should we be wise. In 2023, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) commissioned Walker to create the first site-specific installation for its Roberts Family Gallery. In 2025, Walker was one of the artists commissioned to create a work for MONUMENTS, an exhibition at The Geffen Contemporary at MOCA and The Brick, alongside Bethany Collins, Julie Dash, Karon Davis, Abigail DeVille, Stan Douglas, Kevin Jerome Everson, Kahlil Robert Irving, Monument Lab, Walter Price, Cauleen Smith, and Davóne Tines; all works were newly created and “mark the recent wave of monument removals as a historic moment.” Walker co-curated the exhibit with Hamza Walker, Director of The Brick, and Bennett Simpson, Senior Curator at MOCA. In 1998/1999, Walker designed a large-scale picture (176 m²) for the Vienna State Opera as part of the "Safety Curtain" exhibition series conceived by museum in progress. In 2009, she curated volume 11 of Merge Records' Score!. In 2010, invited by fellow artist Mark Bradford, she developed free lesson plans for K-12 teachers at the J. Paul Getty Museum, offering a lesson where students collaborated on a story by exchanging text messages. In March 2012, Clifford Owens performed a score by Walker at MoMA PS1. In 2013, Walker produced 16 lithographs for a limited edition fine art printing of the libretto Porgy & Bess by DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin, published by the Arion Press. The Detroit Institute of Art removed her work "The Means to an End: A Shadow Drama in Five Acts" (1995) from a 1999 exhibition "Where the Girls Are: Prints by Women from the DIA's Collection" when African-American artists and collectors protested its presence; the five-panel silhouette of an antebellum plantation scene was in the permanent collection and was to be re-exhibited at some point according to a DIA spokesperson. A Walker piece entitled "The moral arc of history ideally bends towards justice but just as soon as not curves back around toward barbarism, sadism, and unrestrained chaos" at the Newark Public Library was questioned by employees regarding its appropriateness for the reading room; the artwork included depictions of the Ku Klux Klan with a burning cross, a naked black woman fellating a white man, and Barack Obama. The piece was covered but not removed in December 2012 and was again uncovered after discussion among employees and trustees. In March 2013, Walker visited the Newark Public Library to discuss the work, addressing themes of racism, identity, and her use of "heroic" figures such as Obama, asking whether these archetypes collapse history, as they are meant to expand the conversation but often do not. Walker described the overwhelming subject matter of her works as a "too-muchness." In the 1999 PBS documentary "I'll Make Me a World," African-American artist Betye Saar criticized Walker's work for its "revolting and negative" depiction of black stereotypes and enslaved people, accusing it of pandering to the enjoyment of "the white art establishment." In 1997, Saar emailed 200 fellow artists and politicians to express concerns about Walker's use of racist and sexist imagery and its positive reception in the art world. This attention led to a 1998 symposium at Harvard University, Change a Joke and Slip the Yoke: A Harvard University Conference on Racist Imagery, which discussed her work. Walker's first museum survey, organized by Philippe Vergne in 2007, was held at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis and traveled to the Whitney Museum in New York, the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles, and the ARC/Musee d'Art Moderne de la ville de Paris. Public collections holding Walker's work include the Minneapolis Institute of Art, the Weisman Art Museum (Minneapolis, Minnesota), the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Tate Collection (London), the Pérez Art Museum Miami, the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, the Madison Museum of Contemporary Art (Madison, Wisconsin), the Menil Collection (Houston), and the Muscarelle Museum of Art (Williamsburg, Virginia); early large-scale cut-paper works have been collected by Jeffrey Deitch and Dakis Joannou. In 1997, at age 28, Walker was one of the youngest recipients of a MacArthur fellowship. Her work received criticism from older generations of African-American artists who accused it of being pornographic and of pandering to racism, targeting a white audience who they believed covertly enjoyed the racist imagery she repurposed. She was the United States representative for the 25th International São Paulo Biennial in Brazil in 2002. Walker received the 2004 Deutsche Bank Prize and the 2005 Larry Aldrich Award. In 2007, she was listed among Time magazine's 100 Most Influential People in the World, Artists and Entertainers, in an essay by artist Barbara Kruger. In 2012, she was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Letters and won the International Artist Award from Anderson Ranch Arts Center in Colorado. In 2016, she was an artist-in-residence at the American Academy in Rome. Walker has been featured on the PBS series Art21: Art in the Twenty-First Century; her work appears on the cover of musician Arto Lindsay's recording "Salt" (2004), and she co-wrote the song "Suicide Demo for Kara Walker" on the Destroyer album "Kaputt." Her name appears in the lyrics of the Le Tigre song "Hot Topic." In 2017, a large-scale mural portrait of Kara Walker by artist Chuck Close was installed in a New York City subway station (Q line, 86th Street) as part of an MTA public arts program. She was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 2018 and to the Royal Academy of Arts in London in 2019 as an Honorary Royal Academician (HonRA). Early in her career, Walker lived in Providence, Rhode Island, with her husband, German-born jewelry professor Klaus Bürgel, whom she married in 1996; she gave birth to a daughter in 1997. The couple separated, and their divorce was finalized in 2010. As of 2017, Walker is in a relationship with photographer and filmmaker Ari Marcopoulos, whom she married in 2025. Walker moved to Fort Greene, Brooklyn, in 2003 and has been a professor of visual arts in the MFA program at Columbia University since then. She maintained a studio in the Garment District, Manhattan, from 2010 until 2017 and moved her art practice to a studio in Industry City in May 2017. She also owns a country home in rural Massachusetts. In addition to her own practice, Walker served on the board of directors of the Foundation for Contemporary Arts (FCA) between 2011 and 2016.
